proofs.proof_tex:
Write \(m_G=1+d/\gamma\) and \(D_F=1+d/\gamma+d/q\).  All constants below are positive, depend only on \(d,\alpha,\beta,\gamma,L,e_0\), and may change from line to line.

First, privacy cannot reduce the nonprivate minimax risk.  For any pure \(\epsilon\)-differentially private Markov kernel \(T\) from \(\mathcal O^n\) to \([-2,2]\), define its conditional barycenter
\[
 \overline T(D_n)=\int_{[-2,2]}t\,T(dt\mid D_n).
\]
The bounded output support makes \(\overline T\) a nonprivate estimator taking values in \([-2,2]\).  Conditional Jensen's inequality gives, for every \(P\in\mathcal M_H\),
\[
 |\overline T(D_n)-\theta(P)|
 \le\int_{[-2,2]}|t-\theta(P)|\,T(dt\mid D_n).
\]
After expectation and supremization over \(P\), the definition of \(R_n^{\mathrm{NP}}\) implies that the risk of \(T\) is at least \(R_n^{\mathrm{NP}}\).  Infimizing over the private kernels in the definition of \(R_{n,\epsilon}^{\mathrm{DP}}\) gives
\[
 R_{n,\epsilon}^{\mathrm{DP}}\ge R_n^{\mathrm{NP}}.
 \tag{28}
\]

For the dense branch, fix a nonnegative smooth bump \(g\), supported on \([-1,1]^d\), with \(g(0)=1\).  For \(0<\Delta\le\Delta_0\), let
\[
 h=c_h\Delta^{1/\gamma},\qquad
 g_h(x)=g\!\left(\frac{x-x_0}{h}\right).
\]
Choose \(c_h\) so that \(\|\Delta g_h\|_{\mathcal H^\gamma}\le L\), and choose \(\Delta_0\) so that \(h\le1/4\) and \(0\le\Delta g_h\le1\).  Since \(x_0\) is interior, the bump is supported in \([0,1]^d\).  Let \(P_0,P_1\) have uniform \(X\), constant propensity \(1/2\), control regression zero, and effects
\[
 \tau_0=0,\qquad \tau_1=\Delta g_h.
\]
Given \(X\), draw binary potential outcomes in \(\{-1,1\}\), independently of \(A\), with the required conditional means, and impose consistency.  Constant propensity, zero control regression, the H\"older scaling, uniform design, and \(e_0\le1/4\) verify every defining property of \(\mathcal M_H\).  Moreover,
\[
 \theta(P_0)=0,\qquad \theta(P_1)=\Delta.
 \tag{29}
\]
Couple one record by using the same \(X,A\) and the monotone coupling of the two binary outcomes.  A mismatch is possible only for \(A=1\), and its conditional probability is \(\Delta g_h(X)/2\).  Therefore
\[
 \Pr(O_0\ne O_1)
 =\frac{\Delta}{4}\int g_h(x)\,dx
 \le C\Delta h^d.
\]
The coordinatewise product coupling has expected Hamming distance
\[
 D\le Cn\Delta h^d\le Cn\Delta^{m_G}.
 \tag{30}
\]
Under \(n\epsilon\ge1\), \(\rho_G=(n\epsilon)^{-1/m_G}\).  Set \(\Delta=c_G\rho_G\), with \(c_G\) small enough that \(\Delta\le\Delta_0\) and \(10\epsilon D\le1\).  Thresholding any private estimator at \(\Delta/2\) is post-processing and gives a pure \(\epsilon\)-private test.  The private Le Cam coupling lemma, with privacy slack zero, gives testing error at least \(0.45e^{-1}\).  By (29), every testing error entails absolute estimation loss at least \(\Delta/2\).  Hence
\[
 R_{n,\epsilon}^{\mathrm{DP}}\ge c\rho_G.
 \tag{31}
\]

For the sparse branch, first suppose \(\rho_F\ge\rho_G\).  Since \(n\epsilon\ge1\), \(n\ge1\), and \(\epsilon\le1\), both caps in the radius definitions are inactive, and
\[
 \rho_F^{D_F}=(n^2\epsilon)^{-1},
 \qquad \rho_G^{m_G}=(n\epsilon)^{-1}.
 \tag{32}
\]
We claim that \(n\rho_F^{d/q}\le1\).  Otherwise, (32) would imply
\[
 \rho_F^{m_G}
 =\frac{\rho_F^{D_F}}{\rho_F^{d/q}}
 <\frac1{n\epsilon}
 =\rho_G^{m_G},
\]
contradicting \(\rho_F\ge\rho_G\), since \(m_G>0\).  This proves the claim.

Set \(\Delta=c_F\rho_F\), with \(c_F>0\) sufficiently small.  The two-fiber distance certificate gives two priors on laws in \(\mathcal M_H\), supported respectively on \(\theta(P)=\Delta\) and \(\theta(P)=0\), at scales
\[
 h\asymp\Delta^{1/\gamma},\qquad
 \ell\asymp\Delta^{1/q}.
\]
The proved inequality \(n\rho_F^{d/q}\le1\) and a sufficiently small \(c_F\) ensure \(n\ell^d\le c_0\), so the certificate supplies a coupling of the prior-predictive samples with
\[
 D\le C\Delta n^2h^d\ell^d
 \le Cn^2\Delta^{D_F}.
 \tag{33}
\]
By (32), \(\epsilon D\le Cc_F^{D_F}\).  Choose \(c_F\) so that \(10\epsilon D\le1\).  Applying the private Le Cam coupling lemma to the two prior predictives and thresholding at \(\Delta/2\) then gives
\[
 R_{n,\epsilon}^{\mathrm{DP}}\ge c\Delta\ge c\rho_F.
 \tag{34}
\]
The construction in the certificate is precisely the asserted smooth shared-sign two-fiber witness and proves the stated Hamming, scale, and occupancy properties.  If \(\rho_F<\rho_G\), (31) already implies a constant multiple of \(\rho_F\).

Taking the smallest of the constants in (28), (31), and (34) proves
\[
 R_{n,\epsilon}^{\mathrm{DP}}
 \ge c_{\mathrm{lower}}\left(R_n^{\mathrm{NP}}\vee\rho_G\vee\rho_F\right).
\]

proposed_core_edits.reason: This verified primary comparator is the closest prior result for the scalar dense pure-central privacy exponent and its one-bump Le Cam lower-bound architecture.

proposed.comparator_claim: Theorem~1 gives the nonprivate pointwise Hölder-CATE lower bound on a class whose covariate density is bounded above; Theorem~2 treats attainability under separate estimator and design conditions.

Theorem~2.1 and Corollary~2 give the one-dimensional uniform-design Gaussian Besov pointwise-MSE rate, while Theorem~4.4, equation~(22), and Section~4.2 give its one-bump Le Cam lower bound.  At \(m=1\), \(\delta=0\), and \(
u=\alpha-1/p\), equation~(22) becomes \(D^{2
u+2}=n^2\epsilon^2\wedge nD\), so the privacy root-MSE scale is \((n\epsilon)^{-
u/(
u+1)}\); for \(d=1\), \(p=\infty\), and comparator smoothness \(
u=\gamma\), this equals \(ho_G\).  The regression experiment is not nested with the bounded potential-outcome CATE experiment and contains neither the \(q=\alpha+ eta\) nuisance interaction nor the \(ho_F\) collision branch.
Section~4 uses treated--control occupancy and effect homogeneity to obtain a global nonprivate rate with a collision term.
The paper stabilizes central-private U-statistics using local Hájek projections and tuple reweighting.
Section~4 gives a general pure-private T-mechanism based on clipped likelihood-ratio tests and finite covers.
The paper gives central-private Le Cam, Fano, and Assouad inequalities based on expected Hamming transport.
Theorems~1 and~3 give finite-query and functional observational CATE releases under approximate differential privacy.

The paper analyzes sample-split differentially private CATE meta-learners and privacy--utility guarantees, but does not establish a pure-central-DP pointwise Hölder minimax converse or an occupancy frontier.
The sparse-histogram lower bound and compact dense-histogram theorem show that pure-private costs can change with representation and occupancy.
Their multiscale and adaptive-lower-bound arguments are templates for the separate unresolved adaptation question; no adaptive rate or logarithmic penalty is imported here.
The paper establishes nonprivate heterogeneous-effect minimax rates with explicit random-design geometry.
Definition~2 and Section~4 construct T-estimators from coherent tests on countable model nets.

prose_updates.related_work:
Kennedy, Balakrishnan, Robins, and Wasserman's Theorem~1 gives the nonprivate pointwise Hölder-CATE lower bound on a class requiring the covariate density only to be bounded above.  Their Theorem~2 addresses attainability under separate estimator and design conditions, including additional local-support requirements; the two theorems are not treated here as defining one class.  The present exact-uniform class is a subclass of the common-support and common-constant Theorem~1 slice: the causal constructions prove the \(ho_G\) and \(ho_F\) privacy lower-bound terms on that subclass, and minimax monotonicity transfers every lower-bound term upward.  No upper bound is transferred.  The closest prior result for the scalar dense exponent is Cai, Chakraborty, and Vuursteen \cite{CaiChakrabortyVuursteen2026Regression}.  In their one-dimensional uniform-design Gaussian nonparametric regression model over Besov balls, Theorem~2.1 summarizes the pointwise-MSE frontier, and Corollary~2 gives its homogeneous-server specialization.  Theorem~4.4 gives the pointwise-MSE lower bound \(D^{-2
u}\wedge1\); its equation~(22) defines \(D\) by \(D^{2
u+2}=\sum_{j=1}^m(n_j^2\epsilon_j^2)\wedge(n_jD)\), with \(
u=\alpha-1/p\), and Section~4.2 proves the bound by a localized one-bump coupling and Le Cam's method.  In the one-server pure-central specialization \(m=1\) and \(\delta=0\), the equation is \(D^{2
u+2}=n^2\epsilon^2\wedge nD\); its privacy-dominated solution gives root-MSE scale \((n\epsilon)^{-
u/(
u+1)}\).  When \(p=\infty\), \(d=1\), and their smoothness \(
u=\alpha\) is identified algebraically with the present effect smoothness \(\gamma\), this is exactly \(ho_G=(n\epsilon)^{-\gamma/(\gamma+1)}\).  Thus neither that scalar dense exponent nor the one-bump Le Cam step is claimed as novel here.  Their Gaussian regression experiment and this bounded-potential-outcome observational CATE experiment are not nested, and their result is one-dimensional and uses pointwise squared loss rather than the present \(d\)-dimensional absolute loss, so it does not imply the present \(ho_G\) CATE theorem.  It also has no treatment mechanism, propensity--outcome interaction \(q=\alpha+ eta\), shared-sign two-fiber mixture, collision occupancy, or \((n^2\epsilon)^{-1/(1+d/\gamma+d/q)}\) branch, and therefore cannot imply the \(ho_F\) lower bound.  The retained contribution is the joint pure-central pointwise-CATE converse, especially the sparse \(ho_F\) branch and its transfer to the Kennedy-Theorem-1 class.  Niu, Nori, Quistorff, Caruana, Ngwe, and Kannan analyze sample-split differentially private CATE meta-learners and their privacy--utility guarantees, but do not give a pure-central-DP pointwise Hölder minimax converse or an occupancy frontier.  Zeng, Balakrishnan, Han, and Kennedy motivate conditioning on realized occupancy; Chaudhuri, Loh, Pandey, and Sarkar motivate stable local projections; and Acharya, Sun, and Zhang supply the private Hamming-coupling inequality used in the converse.  Birgé and Asi, Duchi, Haque, Li, and Ruan provide test-selection templates for the unresolved exact-uniform full-fiber construction.  Schröder, Melnychuk, and Feuerriegel study approximate-private CATE releases rather than this pure-private minimax problem.  Balcer and Vadhan illustrate occupancy-dependent privacy transitions.  Cai, Chakraborty, and Vuursteen's separate adaptation work provides templates only for the downstream open adaptation question: this note claims neither an adaptive rate nor a logarithmic adaptation penalty.  Gao and Han analyze distinct nonprivate random-design geometry.

Kennedy et al. give the nonprivate CATE term, and Acharya et al. give a generic private coupling inequality.  Cai, Chakraborty, and Vuursteen's Theorem~2.1 and Corollary~2 give a one-dimensional uniform-design Gaussian Besov pointwise-MSE frontier; Theorem~4.4, equation~(22), and Section~4.2 give the lower bound and its one-bump Le Cam argument.  Their \(m=1\), \(\delta=0\) specialization has privacy root-MSE scale \((n\epsilon)^{-
u/(
u+1)}\), which equals \(ho_G\) for \(d=1\), \(p=\infty\), and \(
u=\gamma\).  Accordingly, neither the scalar dense exponent nor the one-bump Le Cam step is novel.  That Gaussian regression experiment is not nested with bounded potential-outcome CATE laws, and its dimension and loss differ, so it does not imply this \(ho_G\) CATE lower bound.  It has no treatment/propensity--outcome interaction \(q=\alpha+ eta\), shared-sign two-fiber mixture, collision occupancy, or \(ho_F=(n^2\epsilon)^{-1/(1+d/\gamma+d/q)}\) branch.  Niu et al. analyze sample-split private CATE meta-learners but likewise do not supply this pure-central pointwise Hölder CATE converse.  The new content is the joint causal converse, especially \(ho_F\), together with the Kennedy-class transfer.
